name: Gareth Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Gareth, 43, and I do ordinary electrical repairs and wiring in homes and businesses. I've got a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, years of experience and about average skill, but I'm not a manager. The pay is low, and overtime helps with school costs for our children, ten and twelve; my partner works in a nursery, and we have a mortgage and twenty-two days of expenses saved after car repairs. There are few electrical firms nearby, and I use AI occasionally for a customer explanation after a colleague showed me, checking it before it goes anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say useful tools can stay, but the work still has to pay. I use AI occasionally to make a draft customer explanation less clumsy, after a colleague showed me. I'd be happy if the next big change was simply a week without an emergency call at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry about the mortgage. My ordinary wage is low, and we use some paid overtime for school costs and replacing things that break. We've got twenty-two days of expenses saved after the car repairs, so a month with no extra hours would mean some awkward choices even if AI did very little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the ordinary repair calls in homes and businesses. I'd ask the owner this week which extra hours were actually confirmed for the next month, and budget only from the agreed work. In the first year I'd put ten from each paid overtime shift into the reserve, but only after the mortgage, food and school basics were covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because the household needs more reliability than a busy phone promises. I'm experienced enough not to fear the ordinary faults. A correct test reading doesn't put spare cash in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What has your experience given you at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A vocational certificate, an electrician's licence and enough practice to handle the usual repairs without pretending I'm the best in the trade. I'm 43 and about average at the job, not a manager. I know when a call needs somebody with different skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is relying on those extra hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner works in a nursery and our children are ten and twelve. We have a mortgage and few other electrical firms close enough to be a simple switch. I'd rather plan the real hours than tell my family a full diary means money already earned.

say: I'd keep **useful tools** while asking whether the work still pays reliably.
I'd welcome fewer **dinner-time emergencies** more than another dramatic announcement about AI.
think: Our **low ordinary wage** leaves some school and replacement costs dependent on paid overtime.
With **twenty-two days saved**, a month without extra hours would force difficult choices despite little AI change.
do: Keep completing **ordinary repairs** in homes and businesses through the first year.
Confirm **next month's hours** now and budget only from agreed work.
Save **ten per overtime shift** only after actual payment and essential household costs are covered.
feel: **Anxious** about unreliable extra earnings, while confident with ordinary faults.
S0.quote: I'd rather plan the real hours than tell my family a full diary means money already earned.
fieldNote: His **licensed experience** supports confidence on normal repairs, while low pay and reliance on overtime explain anxiety without making him a junior.
The **new saving** depends on actual paid overtime and covered essentials; neither an expected call nor a busy diary becomes guaranteed income.

steps.text: Keep ordinary repairs while confirming actual paid hours with the owner
Save ten per paid overtime shift only after essential household costs are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'd like to see the new planning tool work on a week we can compare. I don't mind changing a habit when somebody can show me it helps. I'd still tell customers a safe repair takes the time it takes, whatever the booking screen says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This could cut the paid overtime we rely on, even if the normal physical repair work stays. Faster planning might let the owner fit the calls into fewer paid hours, or push us to finish them sooner. With our reserve as small as it is, losing the extras matters to my own household, not just the office staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owner this month for a checked demonstration of the approved AI planning tool using a completed week. If the timings matched the jobs, I'd learn the route-update part with a colleague before using it on live calls. In the first year I'd compare actual paid hours with our budget each month and cancel my paid sports channel now to reduce a fixed bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I want to understand what's changing. A proper demonstration is better than me guessing the tool is either magic or useless. I'd rather learn a workable screen than lose hours while insisting nothing has moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you say the timings didn't match?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fault call taking an hour on the old job sheet and being given twenty minutes in the new draft, without any explanation of what work was removed. I'd show the owner that example. A shorter box on the diary isn't itself a faster repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would learning the route tool guarantee your overtime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I wouldn't put that into our budget. I'd check what I was actually paid. I can be willing to learn and still ask whether the new arrangement leaves my family short.

say: I'd test **planning** against a completed week before changing a habit.
I'd tell **customers** safety work still takes time even when the booking screen is quicker.
think: The **overtime** we rely on could shrink as planning fits calls into fewer paid hours.
Our **small reserve** means losing the extras would hurt my household while physical repair work remained.
do: Request a checked **planning demonstration** on a completed week this month.
Learn **route updates** with a colleague only if the timings match actual jobs.
Cancel the **sports channel** now and compare actual paid hours with the budget monthly during the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about lost overtime, while willing to learn a proven change rather than deny it.
S1.quote: A shorter box on the diary isn't itself a faster repair.
fieldNote: He identifies **overtime exposure** through planning efficiency, preserving the distinction between thinking work and continuing physical repairs.
His **steady adoption** requires demonstration, believable timings and colleague help, without assuming participation protects his wage.

steps.text: Learn approved route updates after a checked completed-week demonstration and colleague guidance
Cancel the paid sports channel now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the family the thinking change comes in 2028 and the capable robots follow around 2031. I'd say our job is to plan the bills, not tell the children learning a trade was a mistake. At work I'd want actual hours discussed before anyone claimed the machines had freed us to do better things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect we'd lose a large share of the ordinary installation hours once capable robots arrived. Repair calls might still come, but I don't expect them to replace all the regular work or the overtime. With twenty-two days saved, the mortgage could be short long before I found a new employer offering enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the sports channel now and ask the owner which paid days and rates were actually confirmed. My partner and I would check our normal budget without overtime this month so the gap was visible. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid repair calls and ask the mortgage lender about support only if real earnings left a shortfall, checking eligibility, fees and later payments before accepting anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a serious fall in earnings when the robots follow. I'm still able to make calls and read an offer, but I've started picturing bills on the fridge at three in the morning. I don't want the children thinking every school expense is what tipped us over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a budget showing a shortfall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bring the real numbers to the owner and ask about confirmed paid work, then discuss actual options with my partner. I wouldn't write a hoped-for shift or lender concession into the totals. We'd need an agreement, not a comforting possibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you give up your licence and start over straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd keep earning through the repairs I could do while the physical work remained. I'd check any real vacancy's pay, paid hours and travel before considering a move. I wouldn't throw away a current wage for somebody's promise of a safer field.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking AI** from capable robots around 2031 when talking with the family.
I'd ask about **actual paid hours** rather than accept claims that machines automatically improve the work.
think: I expect a large **installation-income loss** once robots arrive, without enough replacement repair hours.
Our **twenty-two-day reserve** leaves the mortgage exposed before a suitable alternative wage can be found.
do: Cancel the **sports channel** now and confirm actual days and rates with the owner.
Calculate the **no-overtime budget** with my partner this month, counting no unagreed support.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028 and ask the lender about eligibility and full costs only if real income falls short.
feel: **Alarmed** about a major later earnings loss, with sleeplessness despite still having practical steps.
S2.quote: I wouldn't throw away a current wage for somebody's promise of a safer field.
fieldNote: His **expected large loss** is tied to robot-era installation work, while he keeps actual physical repairs in the first post-2028 year.
The **household plan** excludes hoped-for shifts and unagreed concessions, preserving lender eligibility, fees and later-payment conditions.

steps.text: Cancel the paid sports channel now
Keep actual paid repair calls after 2028 while confirming days and rates
Ask lender about eligibility fees and later costs only if actual income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives me a chance to learn something the firm actually uses, rather than buy a course because the advert sounds urgent. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and robots around 2034. I'd use the time, but I wouldn't tell an apprentice the extra years made the trade safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 48 in 2031, with children about fifteen and seventeen, so we'd still need the wages. My present low base pay and uncertain extras still worry me even with a longer warning. A practical skill could help me earn before the robot date, but it doesn't make the later competition disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owner now about a practical course on maintaining emergency lighting, with a chance to use it on the shop work we already do. I'd enrol only if the fees and class time were paid and the firm offered actual practice; I can't lose wages to collect a certificate. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep paid repair work and use any completed course within my licence and the firm's authorised tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more able to see a sequence: ask, check the offer, learn, then use it. I like teaching linked to a job I recognise. I wouldn't pretend a funded place existed until the owner said yes in terms I understood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the owner offered the fee but unpaid class time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a date that didn't lose paid work or for the class time to be covered. Otherwise I wouldn't enrol on that basis. Unpaid electrical training would still take money from the mortgage and school budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do emergency lighting independently after the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only within the work my licence and the firm's arrangements actually allowed, with whatever checks were needed. A short course doesn't automatically give me every kind of authority. I'd ask exactly what tasks I'd be expected to do before paying or enrolling.

say: I'd choose **teaching linked to work** rather than buy a course because an advert sounds urgent.
I'd use **five years** while explaining that robots around 2034 still change the endpoint.
think: At **48** in 2031, I'd still need wages for children approaching adulthood and the mortgage.
My **low base pay** and uncertain extras remain worrying, and a skill doesn't remove later robot competition.
do: Request an **emergency-lighting course** now linked to shop work the firm already does.
Enrol only with **fees covered**, authorised practice, and either paid class time or dates that cost no wages.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2031 and use completed teaching only within my licence and authorised tasks.
feel: **Anxious** about present earnings, with more time to check an affordable and usable teaching offer.
S3.quote: Unpaid electrical training would still take money from the mortgage and school budget.
fieldNote: His **course plan** is conditional on fees, protected earnings and real practice, rather than treating an inquiry as completed training.
He retains **licence limits** and required checks after the short course, preserving experienced average standing without inventing additional authority.

steps.text: Take lighting course only with covered fees protected wages and actual authorised practice
Keep paid repairs after 2031 within existing licence and authorised tasks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years should let me make some sensible choices without frightening the children every weekend. I'd keep the trade and learn proven changes where they help. I'd still check what the family can afford instead of treating a distant date as a reason to sign for something expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and about 56 when the robots followed, so I can't assume retirement would cover the mortgage. The longer warning gives room for learning, but it doesn't change the fact that we need extra hours for some ordinary costs now. I'd still worry if a month arrived with no overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving ten per actually paid overtime shift only after essentials were covered. I'd seek the lighting course under the same covered-fee, protected-wage and real-practice conditions. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid repairs, review real household income monthly with my partner and compare any posted job offer's pay, paid hours and travel before leaving my current work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the bank balance, with less rush about the machines. I'd enjoy having time to test a change instead of being pushed into it. More warning helps me plan; it doesn't make an unconfirmed shift into money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the monthly review show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether overtime had actually been paid, whether essentials were covered and whether we'd had to use the reserve. I'd rather see a small problem before it became a stack of letters. My partner would see the same figures, not just hear me say work was busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your children's plans because of the long scenario?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask them to take advice and compare course costs when the choices came. I wouldn't cancel their interests or tell them my trade was a guaranteed answer. A decade gives us time to ask better questions before signing anything.

say: I'd use **ten years** for sensible changes without treating every family weekend as an emergency.
I'd learn **proven tools** while checking affordability before expensive commitments.
think: I can't assume **retirement** will cover the mortgage at 53 or when robots follow around 56.
Our reliance on **paid overtime** for some ordinary costs still makes a month without extras worrying.
do: Save **ten per shift** from actually paid overtime only after essential household costs are covered.
Seek the **lighting course** only with covered fees, protected wages and real authorised practice.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2036 and compare written offer pay, paid hours and travel before leaving.
feel: **Anxious** about current finances, with less urgency around distant automation and time to judge proven changes.
S4.quote: More warning helps me plan; it doesn't make an unconfirmed shift into money.
fieldNote: His **baseline anxiety** persists because current extra earnings are uncertain; the longer date does not create cash or assumed pension access.
The **monthly review** uses actual pay and reserve use, while training and job changes retain their material affordability and offer conditions.

steps.text: Save ten per paid overtime shift only after essential costs are covered
Take lighting course only with covered fees protected wages and real authorised practice
Keep actual paid repair work after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect a big installation-income loss when robots follow around 2031, before we've built much reserve. Honest paid hours and practical teaching without lost wages would help. I'd also want actual lender options and job offers explained in full, rather than be told that somebody like me will manage somehow.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the person is counting booked work or money already paid. A busy phone can still leave a quiet bank account. I want my children to see work as worthwhile without learning that every worry has to be hidden at dinner.

headlineQuote: A busy phone can still leave a quiet bank account.
portrait: Gareth is **43**, an experienced licensed electrician with a vocational certificate and average skill, earning low base pay and relying on overtime.
His **partner** works in a nursery, with two school-age children, a mortgage, twenty-two days saved and few nearby electrical firms.
He uses **AI occasionally** after demonstration and checks tools against completed work rather than assuming adoption protects earnings.
His **training plans** preserve covered fees, protected wages and actual authorised practice, while longer timelines retain current overtime and household risks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little reserve-building time before he expects large installation-income losses when robots follow around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **paid hours** and practical teaching without lost wages would make household and learning plans usable.
Fully explained **lender options** and written job offers would help him compare actual choices rather than reassuring guesses.
